events.title: Nader's best state
events.text: Alaska gave Ralph Nader 10 percent for president, his best result anywhere; George W. Bush won by 31 points.

events.title: A Senate appointment
events.text: Governor Frank Murkowski appointed his daughter, Lisa Murkowski, to the U.S. Senate seat he had left.

events.title: Murkowski elected
events.text: Lisa Murkowski won a full Senate term with 48.6 percent, a plurality.

events.title: Stevens convicted
events.text: Eight days before the election, Senator Ted Stevens was convicted on seven felony counts of false statements.

events.title: Begich wins
events.text: Democrat Mark Begich beat Stevens by 3,953 votes, the last Democrat elected to the Senate from Alaska.

events.title: Conviction set aside
events.text: Stevens' conviction was set aside and the charges dropped over prosecutors' misconduct.

events.title: Sullivan, attorney general
events.text: Dan Sullivan became Alaska's attorney general; in 2010 he became natural resources commissioner.

events.title: The write-in
events.text: After losing the Republican primary to Joe Miller, Murkowski won as a write-in, the first such Senate win since 1954.

events.title: Sullivan unseats Begich
events.text: Dan Sullivan beat Senator Mark Begich, 47.96 to 45.83 percent, a margin of 6,014 votes.

events.title: A fisheries leader
events.text: Mary Peltola became executive director of the Kuskokwim River Inter-Tribal Fish Commission in Bethel.

events.title: Murkowski again
events.text: Murkowski was re-elected with 44.4 percent in a four-way race.

events.title: Measure 2 passes
events.text: Voters adopted top-four open primaries and ranked-choice general elections, 50.55 to 49.45 percent.

events.title: Sullivan re-elected
events.text: Sullivan beat Al Gross, an independent backed by Democrats, 53.9 to 41.2 percent.

events.title: Anchorage turns
events.text: Joe Biden carried Anchorage, the first Democrat to do so since 1964; Alaska still voted for Donald Trump by 10 points.

events.title: Don Young dies
events.text: Congressman Don Young of Fort Yukon died in March after 49 years in the House.

events.title: Record dividend
events.text: The Permanent Fund Dividend and an energy relief payment reached a record 3,284 dollars.

events.title: Peltola wins
events.text: In Alaska's first ranked-choice election, Mary Peltola beat Sarah Palin, 51.5 to 48.5 percent: the first Alaska Native in Congress.

events.title: Re-elected by 55
events.text: In November, Peltola beat Palin again, 55.0 to 45.0 percent in the final round.

events.title: Murkowski survives
events.text: Murkowski beat the Trump-endorsed Kelly Tshibaka, 53.7 to 46.3 percent in the final round.

events.title: Willow approved
events.text: The federal government approved the Willow oil project on the North Slope, backed by the whole Alaska delegation.

events.title: A family loss
events.text: Peltola's husband, Gene 'Buzzy' Peltola Jr., died in a plane crash near St. Mary's.

events.title: Yukon salmon moratorium
events.text: The United States and Canada agreed a seven-year halt to Yukon River chinook fishing.

events.title: Begich wins the House
events.text: Nick Begich beat Peltola, 51.2 to 48.8 percent in the final round.

events.title: Repeal fails by 743
events.text: A measure to repeal ranked-choice voting failed by 743 votes after a recount.

events.title: Trump by 13
events.text: Donald Trump carried Alaska by 13.1 points; Peltola won almost 13,000 more votes than Kamala Harris.

events.title: Trump endorses Sullivan
events.text: On 21 July, President Trump endorsed Sullivan for a third term.

events.title: Peltola runs
events.text: On 12 January, Peltola announced her Senate run in a video set on the Kuskokwim River.

events.title: Murkowski backs Sullivan
events.text: Hours later, Senator Murkowski endorsed Sullivan's re-election.

events.title: A second Dan Sullivan
events.text: Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a retired teacher from Petersburg, filed for the Senate as a Republican.

events.title: Court keeps him on
events.text: On 29 June, the Alaska Supreme Court upheld a ruling that he could not be removed from the ballot.

events.title: A toss-up
events.text: On 1 July, the Cook Political Report moved the race to toss-up.

events.title: Primary day
events.text: On 18 August, Peltola led the top-four primary with 49.5 percent to Sullivan's 41.4.

events.title: Energy forum
events.text: On 27 August, the two met at the Alaska Oil and Gas Association's forum in Anchorage.

events.title: Heikes advances
events.text: David Leslie, fourth in the primary, withdrew on 31 August; Gerald Heikes of Palmer took his place.

events.title: Kodiak debate
events.text: On 12 September, Sullivan and Peltola debated fisheries in Kodiak.

events.title: Dividend day
events.text: From 1 October, Alaskans received a 1,200-dollar dividend and energy payment.

events.title: Lean Democratic
events.text: On 6 October, Sabato's Crystal Ball moved the race to Lean Democratic.

events.title: Trump in Wasilla
events.text: On 13 October, President Trump held a rally for Sullivan in Wasilla.

events.title: Early voting
events.text: Early voting runs from 19 October to 2 November.

events.title: Election Day
events.text: On 3 November, Alaskans can rank Sullivan, Peltola, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. and Heikes; ranked-choice counting is set for 18 November.

eras: Sullivan's Senate, a new way to vote
chartNote: Each state is coloured by the margin of the most recent presidential popular vote (Democratic minus Republican share of all votes; FEC and Alaska Division of Elections certified results). It is a simplification: Alaska elects its senator in its own ranked-choice race, and many Alaskans split their tickets (in 2024 Donald Trump won Alaska by 13 points while the Republican House candidate led the first round by 2), so the presidential colour is a backdrop, not a forecast. Shares are of land area, not of people or votes, and Alaska's size dominates them. Boundaries are today's states (Natural Earth); the map is framed on Alaska, so the other states are cut at the edge.
